idiom_name: encode(to:) checks the requested key set carried in JSONEncoder.userInfo
implementation_notes: Foundation has no field-selection mechanism, so the structure is hand-written: pass the caller's field set through JSONEncoder.userInfo (a CodingUserInfoKey), and let the resource's encode(to:) consult it and call the keyed container only for allowed keys. A generic wrapper can forward the container, but the practical form lives on the resource type, where CodingKeys already enumerates the vocabulary - encodeIfPresent covers optional fields without inventing nulls.
pitfalls: The requested set must live in the per-request value, never in a cached/shared model instance - otherwise one caller's selection leaks into the next response.
Reusing the same Codable type for input and output breaks as soon as CodingKeys omit a property: decoding then silently drops the field, and round-trips lose data.
An unknown name in the set produces an empty object rather than an error; validate against CodingKeys or a separate allowlist at the boundary.
encodeIfPresent versus encode changes whether a selected-but-empty field appears as null or vanishes - pick one rule per API and test it.

variants.name: Apollo iOS generated operation models
variants.idiom_name: generated operation models containing only the fields the query selects
variants.implementation_notes: With Apollo iOS the projection is a build-time artifact: each GraphQL operation generates strongly typed models that contain properties only for the selected fields, and the server resolves exactly those. The compiler then rejects any code that touches a field the operation did not ask for, which is partial response by construction rather than by runtime filtering - the client counterpart of a server-side selection set.
variants.code_sketch:
let query = UserCardQuery(id: "42")             // operation selects id + email only
let user = try await apollo.fetch(query: query).data?.user
print(user?.email ?? "-")                      // no property exists for other fields
pitfalls: The selection set is fixed at build time by the app, not by an end user's fields parameter - a server still needs its own selection contract for third parties.
A new field combination requires a new operation document (and a new codegen run); generated models are per-operation, not a general DTO.
The normalized cache can serve fields that the current operation did not select, so 'the model has no property' is not the same as 'the data was never fetched'.
